title: Jude and the Smile
premise: Xanthe Villalobos, a hospice nurse who has spent his life making himself unnoticeable, discovers that every photograph from his late grandmother's house now contains an empty chair that wasn't there before—and the dying patients on his ward have begun counting backwards from a number only he can hear. The chair, he learns, is an invitation his grandmother accepted decades ago to save his life, and the thing that holds the debt has come to collect. To survive until sunrise, Xanthe must stop being invisible, claim his name before the assembled dead, and choose between erasing himself forever or taking his grandmother's place at the table. He survives by finally being seen—but the smile that follows him home knows his name now, and it is patient.
about_author: Yara Dunmore is the pen name of a former hospice volunteer who spent six years listening to the last words of strangers and swears half of them weren't talking to anyone in the room. She lives in a coastal town where the fog arrives earlier each year, and she counts her doors every night.

chapters.title: The Counting Ward
chapters.summary: Xanthe, POV, works the night shift at Rosehaven Hospice, where patient Marisol counts backwards from thirty in a voice not quite her own. He keeps his rituals—lights on, doors counted, himself small. When she reaches zero, she smiles at him and says, 'He's almost done counting you.' The beat: dread disguised as routine.

chapters.title: Grandmother's House, Empty
chapters.summary: Xanthe POV. He returns to his grandmother's house to sort her belongings, three weeks after her funeral. The house feels attentive, like something waiting for him to finish so it can begin. He finds her hospice notebooks—pages of tallies in her handwriting, decades of them, always counting down. The beat: grief laced with wrongness.

chapters.title: The Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Xanthe POV. Going through family photo albums, he notices it: every photograph, back to 1962, now includes a wooden chair against the wall—an empty chair that was never there. In the oldest photo, someone sits in it, blurred beyond recognition. The beat: the past rewriting itself around him.

chapters.title: Doors Counted Twice
chapters.summary: Xanthe POV, back at his apartment. He counts seven doors before bed; at 3 a.m. there are eight. The eighth door is warm to the touch and hums like a held breath. He doesn't open it. In the morning it's gone, but the carpet is dented where something heavy stood. The beat: the invasion of his one safe place.

chapters.title: Marisol's Last Zero
chapters.summary: Marisol POV, her final days. She remembers her own mother counting backwards in a kitchen in Oaxaca, and the tall woman with the patient smile who traded years for favors. Marisol knows what Xanthe is carrying and tries to warn him in fragments: 'Don't answer to the name it gives you.' The beat: tenderness and terror entwined.

chapters.title: What Grandma Signed
chapters.summary: Xanthe POV. In the house's crawlspace he finds a contract written in his grandmother's blood-inked hand, dated the night of his birth: her life extended in exchange for 'the boy, when he is ready to be counted.' He learns he was supposed to die as an infant. The beat: the floor dropping out of his origin story.

chapters.title: The Neighbor Who Remembers
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Elderly neighbor Odell Reyes, the only person who ever truly saw Xanthe, reveals that Grandma Villalobos once hosted 'a dinner' in 1963—a gathering of neighbors who each owed something. Everyone who attended died smiling. Odell refused his invitation and has been half-invisible ever since, a mirror of Xanthe's condition. The beat: recognition between two hidden people.

chapters.title: Sunrise Deadline
chapters.summary: Xanthe POV. Marisol dies at dawn, and in her last breath the backwards counting transfers to him—he now hears it in his own skull, ticking down from 4,000. Odell deciphers the notebooks: the count marks the nights remaining until 'the table is set.' Xanthe has until the count reaches zero. The beat: the clock becomes the antagonist.

chapters.title: The Photograph That Moves
chapters.summary: Xanthe POV. In the oldest photo, the blurred figure in the chair has shifted closer to the camera overnight. Each night it gains definition. He burns the album; by morning the chair appears in photos on his phone, in a magazine, in the hospice's lobby portrait. The thing is not in the pictures—the pictures are in it. The beat: containment fails.

chapters.title: Invisible No More
chapters.summary: Odell POV. Odell teaches Xanthe the mechanics of being unseen—how he's practiced erasure his whole life, and how the entity feeds on exactly that self-erasure. To fight it, Xanthe must do the one thing he fears: be witnessed, named, remembered. He tells his coworkers the truth about the counting. The beat: vulnerability as strategy.

chapters.title: The Dinner Guest List
chapters.summary: Xanthe POV. He finds the 1963 guest list tucked in Grandma's Bible. Nine names, eight crossed out. The ninth is his grandfather—who didn't die smiling, who vanished. The entity's smile, Xanthe realizes, belongs to someone who was once invited too and never left the table. The beat: the monster has a history.

chapters.title: Counting at Work
chapters.summary: Multiple staff POV at Rosehaven. Xanthe's confession has consequences: the backwards counting spreads to other patients, then to the staff break room clock, which now runs in reverse at night. Coworker Dev, who once ignored Xanthe for years, chooses to believe him and stays for the night shift. The beat: belonging forged under siege.

chapters.title: The Eighth Door Opens
chapters.summary: Xanthe POV. The eighth door reappears in his apartment, open this time, revealing his grandmother's kitchen in 1963, mid-dinner, the guests frozen mid-laugh. He steps through and walks among them; they are aware, pleading, trapped in the moment they said yes. His grandmother's young face turns to him: 'Don't sit down.' The beat: the past is a trap still occupied.

chapters.title: Rules of the Table
chapters.summary: Odell POV. Odell's mother attended a similar dinner in her village and left him a list of the entity's rules: it cannot take what is freely witnessed by three; it cannot cross a threshold where its name is spoken; it must honor a seat formally offered and formally refused. The rules are a weapon—but using them requires Xanthe to face it directly. The beat: hope with a price tag.

chapters.title: Zero Approaches
chapters.summary: Xanthe POV. The count passes 500. Patients across the ward count in unison now, and the hospice feels less like a building than a throat. Dev and Odell help Xanthe prepare: salt lines, the contract, the guest list, and a plan to formally refuse the seat at sunrise before the final guest arrives. The beat: grim preparation, found family.

chapters.title: The Smile in the Mirror
chapters.summary: Xanthe POV. The entity stops hiding: it appears in every reflective surface wearing Xanthe's face, smiling with too many years behind it. It speaks in his grandmother's voice, then his own, offering a bargain—sit down willingly and the counting stops, the patients live, and he'll never be invisible again because it will never let him go. The beat: temptation tailored to his deepest wound.

chapters.title: Dev's Vigil
chapters.summary: Dev POV. Dev keeps watch through the worst night, documenting everything in a witness notebook—names, times, what he sees—because three witnesses can bind it. He writes Xanthe's full name on every page, forcing the universe to keep track of him. Xanthe sleeps for the first time in days, held by the fact of being recorded. The beat: being seen as salvation.

chapters.title: The Last Guest
chapters.summary: Xanthe POV. The count reaches single digits. The eighth door opens wide and the table sets itself in Xanthe's living room—nine chairs, and the blurred figure from the photograph now fully visible: his grandfather, hollow-eyed, still smiling, still waiting for someone to take his place so he can finally leave. The beat: the monster is a prisoner too.

chapters.title: Sunrise Refusal
chapters.summary: Xanthe POV, climax begins. At first light, with Odell and Dev as witnesses, Xanthe stands before the table and formally refuses the seat—naming himself, his grandmother's sacrifice, and the debt as fraudulent. The room rebels; the walls become the 1963 kitchen; the frozen guests scream at him to sit and end it. He holds. The beat: defiance at the point of no return.

chapters.title: The Name at the Table
chapters.summary: Climax continues, shifting to the grandfather's fragmented POV inside the entity. Xanthe does the unthinkable: he speaks his grandfather's name—lost for sixty years—and witnesses him, truly sees him, breaking the entity's claim. The smile cracks. The grandfather rises from the chair for the first time since 1963. The beat: compassion as the killing blow.

chapters.title: What the Sunrise Took
chapters.summary: Xanthe POV. The table burns like paper; the counting reaches zero and stops—not with his death, but with the debt's. His grandfather dissolves into morning light with something like gratitude. The eighth door closes for good. But in the last photograph on his phone, taken at sunrise, there is a faint smile in the window glass. The beat: victory shadowed by cost.

chapters.title: Xanthe, Seen
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Xanthe POV, months later. He keeps the hospice job, keeps the rituals, but no longer keeps himself small—Dev and Odell are family now, and Marisol's plaque hangs by the ward door. He still counts the doors each night. There are seven. He has learned to live with the knowledge that somewhere, something polite and patient is always taking new reservations—and that belonging, not invisibility, is what kept him alive. The beat: hard-won peace, vigilance retained.
